C0.quote: compare voting rules in terms of the expressive utility
C0.note: Compares single-winner voting rules (plurality, approval, A-Borda) via a model of expressive utility and turnout, plus an experiment. Borderline, but coded eligible as the main object is the voting rules and the ballots they allow.

C1.quote: We then ran an online experiment testing this implication
C1.note: Conceptual model with one proposition (expressive power ordering, OT), plus a large online experiment (EM). Most results are experimental.

C2.1.quote: Individual i’s expressed preference, denoted Rei, is the ranking that i casts when voting.

C2.2.note: Expressed preferences are modelled as reflexive, transitive (weak) orders. Rules take plurality, approval and point-score ballots (A-Borda) as inputs. CARD covers the point scores in A-Borda (2/1/0), though these are mapped to ordinal preferences.

C2.3.quote: Individual i’s actual preference, denoted Rai, is the individual own ranking of alternatives.

C2.4.quote: Even so, Rai and Rei may differ.
C2.4.note: Separate notation for actual and expressed preferences.

C3.1.quote: Assume that voters are attentive and sincere
C3.1.note: The theoretical model assumes sincere voters, but the empirical analysis allows non-sincere voting and discusses strategic voting and noise. Coded SOME.

C3.2.quote: voters are attentive and sincere, in the sense that they do not make mistakes

C3.3.quote: they vote as closest as possible to their actual preference
C3.3.note: The sincerity assumption is given without a reason.

C4.1.quote: Ei (Rei ) denotes i’s expressive utility of voting Rei.
C4.1.note: Expressive utility is defined as a function of the Kemeny distance between expressed and actual preference. Material benefit B_i is mentioned but not tied to the ballot beyond the preferred option in Rei.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.quote: differences in expressive power can have a significant impact in terms of the representation
C5.1.note: Experiment evaluates rules by representation of voters' actual preferences (Kemeny distance) and expressive utility.

C5.2.quote: Kemeny distance between participants’ actual and expressed preferences
C5.2.note: Evaluated against separately elicited actual preferences.

VOT.quote_behav: around 30% of subjects did not vote sincerely
VOT.note: Model assumes sincere voters. Experiment discusses strategic and non-sincere voters and the turnout decision. Information about others is not specified.

ORG.note: Experimenters set the rules. Not an agent in the model.

C8.1.note: Strategic voting is mentioned as a possible confounder but no solution concept is used. VOT is MIXED, so C8 nominally applies, but no concept is analysed. Codes left empty.

claims.quote: expressive power of voting rules is a relevant criterion when deciding which voting rule to use
a voting rule with higher expressive power is desirable
the government could link the reform with an informational campaign

C9.2.note: The needed assumptions are stated: the link between expressed and actual preferences via the expressive utility function, ceteris paribus, and awareness of alternative rules. The generalisation 'if this holds more generally' is hedged.

C10.1.note: The paper explicitly distinguishes actual and expressed preferences.
